title: Competence vs Perfection
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that teacher Credibility in students' eyes depends on competence, not perfection, and lays out eight specific domains where competence reliably pays off. He splits the domains into two groups: four practiced during instruction (classroom stewardship, student motivation, lesson preparation, and the science of learning) that have the most immediate effect on Credibility, and four practiced outside instruction (content/pedagogy knowledge, stress management, working with adults, and time management) that build Credibility more slowly but still matter. He's candid that he is not perfect in any of the eight domains himself, framing the list as a map for ongoing self-improvement rather than a scorecard of failure. The piece closes with a compact thesis that reframes the goal of teacher growth: not flawlessness, but demonstrable, growing competence across a known set of areas.
points: Reframes teacher Credibility as a function of competence, not perfection - students' hearts are "more gracious" than teachers assume.

Organizes eight competence domains into two tiers by proximity to instruction: in-class domains (classroom management, motivation, lesson prep, science of learning) affect Credibility fastest; out-of-class domains (content knowledge, stress management, working with adults, time management) build it more slowly.
Models vulnerability by admitting to being "perfect in exactly zero" of the eight domains, positioning the framework as a growth map rather than a judgment tool.
Closes with a compact, quotable thesis - "Perfection is not the goal. Competence is." - that reduces the whole argument to a single actionable standard.
quotes: Something a lot of us teachers need reminding of is that becoming Credible in the eyes of a student has little to do with becoming a perfect teacher or doing everything at the level of total excellence.
Instead, our students' hearts are much more gracious than this; they long not for our perfection but for our competence.

Classroom Stewardship/Management - that is, understanding the group psychology of the classroom and the methods that work best for creating a learning-conducive environment in which everyone feels heard, known, valued, and safe.
And with all this, it's critical to grasp that perfection isn't what you're after. I'm perfect in exactly zero of the domains pictured above.

But, by focusing my self-improvement efforts over the last handful of years, I do think I've grown increasingly competent in all of these areas, and that has made both my job and the jobs of my students much more effective and enjoyable.
